A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GENERATE ANY SCENE, with matching authors, taxonomy, and retained experimental blocks. The text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial rewriting and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D evaluations, alongside self-improvement, targeted distillation, and generated-content detection experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds reinforcement-learning experiments, alternative-data comparisons, full fine-tuning experiments, paraphrase testing, and human evaluation.

M1.justification: The four-step caption-generation pipeline in v1 gains a fifth step that generates question-answer pairs directly from scene graphs. v3 Sections 2.1 and 5 use these pairs with Qwen2.5-VL-3B to compute an accuracy-based reward for GRPO training of SimpleAR. This introduces a substantive training route beyond the retained self-improvement, distillation, and detection procedures.

E1.justification: v3 adds DPG-Bench and GenEval evaluation, covering explicit compositional requirements such as object presence, position, and color binding. Training comparisons additionally use MS-COCO-2017 and LAION-COCO captions, retrieved real images for multi-object and hard-concept captions, and VQAv2 question-answer annotations matched to COCO captions. The paraphrase study also tests linguistic variation for retained scene content; the original image, video, and 3D coverage remains.

E2.justification: v3 adds MS-COCO-2017 and LAION-COCO fine-tuning baselines, web-retrieved images as an alternative to DALL-E 3 distillation data, and SimpleAR SFT, CLIP-reward, and VQAv2-reward comparisons. The general evaluation also adds KLING 1.6 and Wanx 2.1 in Table 4 and Meshy-4 in Table 6. These are reported comparison entries, rather than citation-only additions.

E3.justification: New protocols include one-epoch SimpleAR GRPO training on 10K synthetic captions versus the CLIP baseline's 11K real-data captions, full fine-tuning across three iterations, and distillation on FLUX.1-dev. Appendix A.3 adds a 100-graph paraphrase test and six-model human evaluation with three judges assessing 40 groups each. Table 3 also changes FLUX1.1 PRO's reported evaluation size from v1's 10K-caption table description to a 1K subset; unchanged scores do not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of sensitivity to caption phrasing, agreement with human judgments, dependence on LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and the effectiveness of alternative distillation data. Appendix E.3 compares scene-graph rewards with VQAv2-based rewards, while Figure 17 examines training reward progression. The earlier complexity, plausibility, fairness, metric, and fine-grained category analyses are retained in Appendix A.4.

E5.justification: v3 adds inter-annotator reliability reporting: three evaluators assess ten shared groups, with reported Spearman agreement of 0.962 in Appendix A.3.2. This is a limited addition to statistical reporting. Neither version reports training-seed replications, confidence intervals, or significance tests for model-performance differences.

E6.justification: Most earlier benchmark and detector scores are retained, but v3 adds substantial new results. Table 2 reports DPG overall scores of 80.50 for the proposed RL model and 79.66 for CLIP-RL; Table 10 reports third-iteration full fine-tuning VQA scores of 0.540 versus CC3M's 0.519. The self-improvement headline changes from 5% to 4% while its original plot remains. Tables 12 and 13 report identical original and distilled scores for SDv1.5 and FLUX.1-dev, an unexplained duplication.

T1.justification: The scene-graph representation and element-count definition of complexity are retained. Neither version supplies theorems, proofs, or formal guarantees; the added reward and GRPO material describes procedures without introducing a mathematical derivation or theoretical analysis.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds comprehensive evaluation of realistic and imaginative scenes, whereas v3 foregrounds structured data synthesis for visual-generation training. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add automatic QA generation and low-cost reward modeling as central contributions, expanding three applications to four. The claimed self-improvement changes from 5% to 4%, and v1's explicit ten-million-caption release claim is omitted.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning phrasing robustness, human alignment, independence from LoRA, and generalization beyond CC3M. It attributes web-image fine-tuning failures to noise and caption mismatch, and VQAv2 reward weaknesses to incomplete alignment between captions and questions. Appendix G adds curriculum-based GRPO as a future direction. The original implausibility and linguistic-diversity limitations are largely retained after relocation, while the introduction's explicit higher-order relationship limitation is omitted.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the paraphrasing prompt, additional graph-control documentation, and substantial RL implementation information, including metadata filtering, reward evaluator, learning schedule, vLLM settings, eight H100 GPUs, and approximately 14 hours of training. It also describes sourcing the new image and QA baselines. The dataset access link changes from an individual dataset to a collection; the code link and original LoRA and detector settings are retained.

R1.justification: v3 substantially extends the positioning toward structured training data, autoregressive visual generation, and semantic reward modeling, adding discussion and citations involving LAION-SG, SimpleAR, T2I-R1, Janus, Janus-Pro, RLHF, and GRPO. ProVision and m&m's references present in v1 are removed. Robin and Synthetic Visual Genome are matched as the retained relationship-data source across the reference update.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and opening motivation are extensively rewritten around training. Methods and applications move ahead of the comprehensive evaluation, related work moves toward the end, and the appendices are reorganized to consolidate evaluation and analyses. Application descriptions and terminology are also rewritten, making this a substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting, removes the original application-overview figure, and redraws the generation pipeline to include QA production. v3 adds reward-training and qualitative-comparison figures and several experimental tables. Existing benchmark displays move into the appendix, and four separate category-comparison figures become panels of Figure 14.

improvement.justification: The equal-budget real-caption baselines and full fine-tuning controls in Appendix C strengthen v1's reliance on CC3M and LoRA alone, providing a modest net improvement. Human evaluation and added implementation details also help. However, new reporting defects limit the gains: Table 2's 80.50 versus 79.66 does not support the abstract's +5% DPG claim; Table 7's reported 0.9232 correlation matches scores, whereas its printed ranks yield approximately 0.8182; and the identical SDv1.5 and FLUX.1-dev entries in Tables 12–13 remain unexplained. These issues prevent a substantial overall quality improvement.
